s01-title: Video seven: multi-tenancy. One server, many companies.
s02-list: Same URL, same DocType, two companies. The demo account belongs to both tenants. Each pane calls the same API with a different X Astra Tenant header: Saigon has three customers, Hanoi has two.
s03-form: Same document code, but C zero zero one in Saigon is not C zero zero one in Hanoi. Each tenant has its own record, even with the same code.
s04-resolve: No API takes the tenant as a parameter. The kernel tries header, subdomain, then the user's only tenant. Unresolved: four hundred. Non-members: four oh three. Then it rides a scoped value into the PostgreSQL transaction.
s05-links: Links respect tenants. C zero zero one is a different customer in each tenant. C zero zero three exists only in Saigon: Hanoi gets four oh four, and an order using it fails.
s06-members: Members only. User Nam, a Hanoi admin, calls Saigon: four oh three. User demo is in two tenants and sends none: four hundred. Fail-closed: if it is ambiguous, the kernel refuses.
s07-rls: If you forget to set the tenant, the application role sees zero rows. Set the Saigon tenant inside a transaction, and it sees that tenant's data. Force row level security applies to the table owner too.
s08-code: For developers: the tenant follows the flow, not a parameter, from scoped value to transaction. At startup, Row Level Security Guard stops the kernel if the role is superuser or bypasses RLS. Details in video eight.
s09-recap: Four layers of isolation: one URL, Links, Keycloak per tenant, and zero rows without a tenant. Next: fail-closed security.
s10-outro: Astra. One platform, every business process. Open source, MIT license.
